data.text:
I ran searches for all four claims. Claim 0 is supported with a small correction to the framing. Claims 1 and 2 are supported as written. Claim 3 is supported, but the "arrives first" detail rests on a weaker source than I'd like. The URLs below are the sources I relied on.

**Claim 0: Cessna 172 takeoff ground roll of about 300 m (960 ft) at sea level, max weight**
- **AOPA aircraft guide for the 172S:** Takeoff distance ground roll is 960 ft, takeoff distance over a 50-ft obstacle is 1,630 ft, and rate of climb at sea level is 730 fpm. URL: https://www.aopa.org/go-fly/aircraft-and-ownership/aircraft-guide/aircraft/cessna-172
- **Cessna 172S Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH), Section 1:** It lists takeoff performance "Ground Roll … 960 FEET" and a maximum takeoff weight of 2550 pounds. URL: https://www.befa.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/POH-Cessna-172S.pdf
- **Flyaway Simulation:** This is a secondary source. It gives 960 ft as about 293 m of ground roll. That makes "roughly 300 m" fair. URL: https://flyawaysimulation.com/ask/answers/cessna-runway-length-takeoff-landing/
- **Verdict: supported, with a small correction.** The figure is for the 172S model (180 hp). The POH conditions (sea level, max weight, standard day, flaps, runway surface) weren't visible in the snippets I retrieved. Older 172s with less power have different numbers. Suggested wording: "A Cessna 172S needs about 960 ft (≈293 m) of ground roll at sea level, per its handbook."

**Claim 1: Flaps let a plane lift off and land at lower speed and in shorter distance**
- **AOPA, "How It Works: Flaps":** Flaps typically lower an airplane's stall speed and allow steeper descent angles without gaining speed. They usually shorten the ground roll at the expense of a lower rate of climb. Full flaps allow slower approach speeds and steeper approach angles. URL: https://www.aopa.org/news-and-media/all-news/2018/february/flight-training-magazine/how-it-works-flaps
- **Wikipedia, "Flap (aeronautics)":** Using flaps on takeoff reduces ground roll but also reduces the climb rate. The 172S POH recommends 10° of flaps on takeoff for soft ground or a short runway, otherwise 0°. URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flap_(aeronautics)
- **Verdict: supported as written.** One nuance is that flaps help takeoff roll but cost climb rate. For landing, the shorter distance comes from the lower approach speed.

**Claim 2: A wing lifts by deflecting air downward, pushing the wing up (Newton's third law)**
- **NASA, "The Wing's the Thing" (hosted on hiller.org):** A wing creates lift in part by deflecting air downwards and in part due to the pressure difference, in keeping with Newton's Third Law. The text also says the airflow is turned downwards as the wings strike the air at an angle. URL: https://www.hiller.org/wp-content/uploads/docs/TheWingsTheThing_v2.pdf
- **AvWeb, "Theories of Lift":** Both Bernoulli's principle and Newton's laws (action-reaction from downward air deflection) contribute to lift, though each is incomplete individually. URL: https://avweb.com/features/theories-of-lift/
- **Verdict: supported as written.** If you want to be precise, NASA describes it as "in part" deflection and "in part" pressure difference. These are two descriptions of the same physics, not competing causes. You could add "…and the pressure difference around the wing is the other side of the same effect."

**Claim 3: Air over the top reaches the trailing edge before the air below, so equal transit time is wrong**
- **NASA Glenn, "Incorrect Lift Theory #1":** The "Longer Path" or "Equal Transit Time" theory is described as one of the most widely circulated incorrect explanations. A symmetric airfoil, with upper and lower surfaces the same length, still generates plenty of lift. The page says that it is the flow turning that matters, not the distance. URL: https://www.grc.nasa.gov/www/k-12/VirtualAero/BottleRocket/airplane/wrong1.html (also mirrored at https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Equal_transit-time_NASA_wrong1.gif)
- **Angle of Attack (pilot education site):** It calls the equal-transit idea a myth and says the air over the top actually arrives first. URL: https://www.angleofattack.com/what-is-bernoullis-principle-in-aviation/
- **Verdict: supported.** The part that equal transit time is wrong is firmly supported by NASA. The retrieved NASA text didn't include an explicit "arrives first" sentence. That detail comes from the pilot-education site, which is not a government or engineering source. I'd cite NASA for "wrong" and treat "arrives first" as well-established but secondarily sourced. Suggested wording: "Air over the top gets to the back edge first, so the 'equal transit time' explanation is wrong."
